reviewSession.heading: What this domain is really about
reviewSession.body:
Let us go back over the whole of this domain before your exam. Domain 6 is about proving that security really works. A control that exists on paper is only a hope until someone tests it, records the result and acts on it.

Hold on to the flow of the domain. First you plan the checks. Then you carry out the tests. You collect data about your security routines. You analyze the results and report them. And you support audits.

The exam wants the judgment of a manager and an adviser, more than the skill of a technician. So when a question feels technical, step back. Ask what the business needs, who has the authority to decide, and whether people are safe. Fix causes and not symptoms. And remember that finding a problem is never the end of the job.

reviewSession.heading: Strategy, and who does the checking
reviewSession.body:
Now the first objective, strategy. A strategy starts from business goals, risk and legal duties. It never starts from a tool. Validating a strategy means confirming that the plan itself is still right, especially after a merger or a move to the cloud.

Do not mix up three words. A test checks one control. An assessment is wider and ends with advice. An audit is formal, independent and evidence-based, against a fixed standard.

On who does the work, internal is within your organization's control. External is outside your organization's control. Third-party is outside your enterprise's control, such as a regulator. Independence and cost generally rise along that line.

For location, on-premises lets you test nearly everything. In the cloud, read the contract and the provider's rules first. In hybrid, remember the link between the two sides. And with vendors, you can hand over the work but never the accountability.

reviewSession.heading: Scans, CVE and CVSS
reviewSession.body:
Let us review vulnerability work. A vulnerability assessment finds weaknesses and lists them. A penetration test tries to use them. A credentialed scan logs in, so it sees more and is more accurate.

A false positive reports a problem that is not real. A false negative misses a real one, and it is the more dangerous error.

Here is a mix-up the exam loves. CVE, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, names a flaw. CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, scores it. Learn the bands exactly. None is 0.0. Low is 0.1 to 3.9. Medium is 4.0 to 6.9. High is 7.0 to 8.9. Critical is 9.0 to 10.0.

Then remember that a score is general. If a question offers a high score on an isolated test machine and a lower score on a public payment server, the business risk decides. The payment server usually comes first.

reviewSession.heading: Penetration tests, boxes and team colors
reviewSession.body:
On penetration testing, written approval from senior management comes first, together with rules of engagement. Without permission, a test is a crime. If a tester causes an outage or finds a real attacker, the tester stops and calls the named contact.

The four phases in the guide from the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, are planning, discovery, attack and reporting. Attack can loop back to discovery when new systems come into view.

Box types tell you how much the tester knows. White box is full knowledge. Gray box is partial knowledge, such as a normal login. Black box is zero knowledge.

Team colors describe roles. Red attacks. Blue defends. Purple is red and blue sharing what they learn. White referees the exercise.

If a question asks how to measure the real response of the defenders, think of a double-blind test. If it asks how to improve detection, think of purple. And never confuse a white team with a white box.

reviewSession.heading: Logs, synthetic transactions and real users
reviewSession.body:
Next, other control tests. Log reviews depend on synchronized clocks, usually through Network Time Protocol. Logs must also be protected, collected centrally and read by someone. A clipping level ignores events below a set limit.

Now here is another comparison to get exactly right. A synthetic transaction is a scripted, pretend action with a known correct result. It is active, it runs on a schedule, and it needs no real users. So it can warn you at three in the morning. Real user monitoring is passive. It watches what real people do, so it reflects real devices and real locations, but it needs traffic.

If the question says even when nobody is online, choose synthetic. If it says what real customers are experiencing, choose real user monitoring.

A benchmark compares a system with a fixed reference, such as a past baseline or a secure settings guide.

reviewSession.heading: Code, coverage, interfaces and simulations
reviewSession.body:
Let us finish control testing. The Fagan inspection has six steps in order: planning, overview, preparation, inspection, rework and follow-up.

Static testing reads code that is not running. Dynamic testing checks a running program. Fuzz testing sends unexpected input to a running program. Mutation fuzzing changes real input, and generation fuzzing builds input from knowledge of the format.

A misuse case asks how a system could be abused.

Coverage is the number of items tested, divided by the total, times 100. The types are branch, condition, function, loop and statement. High coverage shows what was tested, but it does not prove security.

Interface testing covers the user interface, the network interface and the application programming interface. Use good, bad and boundary values.

Breach attack simulation is automated and repeated, and it shows whether defenses still respond. A compliance check compares controls with a requirement. Remember that compliant does not always mean secure.

reviewSession.heading: Process data, KPIs and KRIs
reviewSession.body:
Now security process data, which shows whether routines are really happening. It can be technical or administrative.

For accounts, check joiners, movers, leavers and privileged accounts. Privilege creep is access that builds up as people change jobs. If leavers keep appearing, deleting those accounts deals with the symptom. Fix the link between human resources and account removal.

For management review, the approver needs real authority and must not be the requester. A signature without reading is worth nothing.

Here is the comparison to get exactly right. A Key Performance Indicator looks back and asks how well we did, such as 95 percent patched on time. A Key Risk Indicator looks ahead and warns that danger is growing, such as unpatched internet-facing servers rising from 2 to 9.

The mirror shows where you have been, and the headlights show what is coming. Reports for senior leaders should show trends, targets and the decisions needed.

reviewSession.heading: Backups, training and recovery tests
reviewSession.body:
Let us review the remaining process data. A backup log shows that a job ran. Only a test restore proves that the data can be recovered, and it also shows how long that takes.

For people, awareness helps them notice danger, training teaches a skill and education builds understanding. Completing a course proves attendance. Changed behavior, such as fewer clicks and more reports of false messages, proves learning.

Disaster recovery brings technology back, and business continuity keeps important work going. People's safety always comes first.

Know the plan tests in order, from least to most disruptive: read-through, structured walk-through, simulation, parallel and full interruption. In a parallel test, the main site keeps running. In a full interruption, it really stops.

The Recovery Time Objective is about how long a system may be down. The Recovery Point Objective is about how much data may be lost, measured in time. Check each one separately against the test result.

reviewSession.heading: Analysis, exceptions and disclosure
reviewSession.body:
Now analysis and reporting. Raw output is not a report. Confirm the results, remove false positives, find common causes, rate the business risk, recommend actions and report them.

Remediation needs an owner, a due date, change management and a retest. A finding is not closed until the fix has been verified. Fix the cause and not just the symptom.

When a fix is not possible, use a formal exception. It needs compensating controls, the approval of the risk owner and an expiry date. Removing a system from scan scope to make a finding disappear is always wrong.

For a flaw in someone else's product, coordinated disclosure is the usual best answer. Tell the vendor privately, allow fair time, then publish. Full disclosure arms attackers, and nondisclosure leaves users exposed.

And the ISC2 canons come in order, starting with protecting society. Give each audience what it needs: leaders get business risk, and technical teams get the details.

reviewSession.heading: Audits and SOC reports
reviewSession.body:
Now audits. Evidence must be sufficient, reliable and relevant. Evidence the auditor gathers directly is stronger than a spoken statement. The auditor chooses the sample. Auditors must never audit their own work, and they ideally report to the audit committee. Auditors advise, and management owns the fix.

When you facilitate an audit, give honest evidence, one point of contact and escorted access. Never alter a record.

Now SOC reports, which stand for System and Organization Controls. SOC 1 covers controls that affect financial reporting. SOC 2 covers security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy, in detail, for permitted readers. SOC 3 is a general summary that may be made public.

Type 1 checks design at one point in time. Type 2 checks design and operating effectiveness over a period, so it gives stronger assurance. Think of a photograph and a video. Match the report to the question, and read its scope, period and exceptions.

reviewSession.heading: How to choose the best answer
reviewSession.body:
Let us end with how to choose. Many questions in this domain offer several good actions, and you must find the best one.

First, look at the word that sets the task, such as first, best or most. Second, ask where we are in the process. Planning and approval come before testing. Confirming comes before reporting. Retesting comes before closing.

Third, be suspicious of answers that are fast but skip the process. Testing without permission, closing without verifying and hiding a finding are almost always wrong.

Fourth, be careful with answers that are technically impressive but ignore the business. A manager thinks about risk, authority and cause.

Finally, check the exact pairs. CVE names, and CVSS scores. Synthetic is active, and real user monitoring is passive. KPI looks back, and KRI looks ahead. Type 1 is design at a moment, and Type 2 is operation over time. Take your time, and trust your reasoning.
